name: Tridens

project_scope.note: Only three Tridens species are manifest-backed; historical source-pool names may map to Tridentopsis. All three retain provisional range labels.

look_here_first: Examine panicle branching first; then glume-to-lemma proportions and lemma hairs under magnification.
shared_traits: Perennial grasses with panicles of multi-flowered spikelets
Glumes and three-nerved lemmas useful for confirmation

comparison_matrix.albescens: Dense, narrow, branches crowded or appressed
comparison_matrix.texanus: Flexuous branches with basal sections bare of spikelets
About half as long as lemmas

comparison_matrix.albescens: Glabrous or hairy only at extreme base
comparison_matrix.flavus: Hair lines along lower portions of nerves

comparison_matrix.albescens: Dense seedhead color varies from green to purple to white
comparison_matrix.flavus: Flattened overlapping basal sheaths; panicle branches sometimes sticky
comparison_matrix.texanus: Spikelets often purple or rose-purple; can resemble Eragrostis secundiflora

overlap_cautions: The provisional T. texanus species record says narrow panicle; regional flora describes flexuous branches bare basally. Needs targeted review.
Panicle length and plant height overlap; confirm glume and lemma anatomy.
Historical Tridens buckleyanus, eragrostoides and muticus source-pool names require accepted-concept mapping; do not add duplicate species cards.

Matched lemma dorsal surfaces at 10–20×; label pubescence along three nerves
T. flavus flattened basal sheaths and collar/ligule
T. albescens dense panicle and near-glabrous lemma
T. texanus versus Eragrostis secundiflora spikelet close-ups

visual_lesson.title: Tridens: the grass ID is in the spikelets
visual_lesson.look_here_first: Follow one complete flowering stem: first compare panicle silhouette and bare lower branch sections, then dissect a spikelet to compare glume length with lemmas and inspect lemma-nerve hairs. Color alone is unreliable.

steps.title: 1 · Read the panicle outline
steps.plain: Are branches tightly crowded, broadly open and drooping, or flexuous with bare bases?
steps.why: T. albescens tends narrow/dense; T. flavus broadly open; T. texanus flexuous with basal gaps.
steps.photo_role: same-scale whole panicles of three exact species

steps.title: 2 · Find the bare branch base
steps.plain: Look for a stretch of branch without attached spikelets.
steps.where: Base of a lateral panicle branch
steps.why: Supports T. texanus but needs cross-check with branch development and other species.
steps.photo_role: T. texanus versus T. albescens and T. flavus branch-base macros

steps.title: 3 · Open a spikelet
steps.plain: The outer pair of bracts are glumes; count the florets and compare their lemmas.
steps.where: Dissected mature spikelet under hand lens with millimeter scale
steps.why: Glume-to-lemma proportions and floret counts help resolve overlapping panicle sizes.
steps.photo_role: matched dissected spikelets of three species

steps.title: 4 · Inspect three lemma nerves
steps.plain: Follow each raised line on the lemma and check where tiny hairs occur.
steps.why: Nerve hair distribution helps separate nearly glabrous T. albescens from hairier T. flavus and T. texanus.
steps.photo_role: matched dorsal lemma macros with verified labels

comparison_cards.title: White tridens versus purpletop
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Dense, narrow versus broad open panicle; confirm by basal sheath and lemma hair patterns.
comparison_cards.caution: Panicle color is variable; photograph whole stalk and dissected lemma.

comparison_cards.title: Texas tridens versus purpletop
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Find the long bare base of flexuous panicle branches and compare with the larger open purpletop panicle.
comparison_cards.caution: Panicle lengths overlap; use glume:lemma ratio and lemma pubescence.

comparison_cards.title: Texas tridens versus lovegrasses
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Dissect spikelet for Tridens lemma nerve architecture rather than relying on pinkish seedhead color.
comparison_cards.caution: Eragrostis secundiflora can resemble T. texanus in the field.
